summary: Redwood delivered an Optimize-focused walkthrough highlighting the cost simulator and several KV/prefix caching strategies to reduce token spend. Customer is evaluating tradeoffs between hosted and dedicated modes, looking for predictable tail latency under 250ms p50 and an SLO of 500ms p95. Action items include a sandbox run and shared cost scenarios.
topics: batch sizing and batch window tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Ava Martinez: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we have about 50 minutes, quick intros then we jump into the cost-simulator and a couple of KV/prefetch strategies, if that's ok.
[00:10] Maya Singh: sounds good, we really want to see numbers for our 1k qps-ish burst pattern, and how prefetching affects our token bill.
[00:20] Kenji Ito: great, i'll share screen, the simulator has three baseline scenarios — hosted standard, hosted with prefetching + batching, and dedicated reserved. i'll pull up our sample run from a similar retail workload to show math.
[00:34] Carlos Ruiz: one quick thing — our infra team needs to know about VPC peering and if KV prefetch stores any customer PII, so that's both security and residency.
[00:43] Rina Shah: noted, we'll cover the KMS + retention bits at the end; the prefix KV prefetch stores only model cache keys, not raw convo. but we can show the data flow diagram.
[00:55] Kenji Ito: ok screen is live, you can see the input fields: QPS, avg prompt tokens, avg response tokens, sessionization TTL, batch window ms. The default prefetch TTL is 30s in the simulator which gave about 18% token savings in this example.
[01:12] Zoe Park: can you explain TTL a bit? we have sessions that are idle for 2–10 minutes on average.
[01:20] Kenji Ito: TTL is how long the prefix KV entries are kept hot — if your session returns within TTL, you avoid recomputing initial prompt prefixes and the KV cache hits reduce repeat compute. For 2–10min idle, we'd recommend a longer TTL but with differential TTL per user segment to control memory and evictions.
[01:38] Omar Patel: memory on dedicated boxes is finite — how does prefetch affect GPU memory and can it bump other working sets?
[01:46] Kenji Ito: good question, prefetch primarily uses KV store memory (RAM backed) and GPU KV cache is cached per-host; we show expected RAM and GPU KV footprints in the simulator. For heavy tails we recommend a session-affinity policy and small LRU window to protect core model memory.
[02:05] Ava Martinez: i want to jump to the numbers — mid-sim, we observed p50 latency improved by ~40ms with prefetch and batching, p95 improved 20–30ms, and cost per 1M tokens dropped roughly 12–22% depending on batch sizing. those ranges are important because batching helps unit cost but can add average latency if the batch window is too long.
[02:28] Maya Singh: 12–22% is promising. our main concern is tail latency for interactive UI — we need p95 < 500ms.
[02:36] Kenji Ito: understood. in the sim i set the batch window to 12ms which keeps p95 within 480ms; with 25ms batch window you save more tokens but p95 creeps to ~550–600ms for our test model. so it's a tradeoff.
[02:53] Leah Bennett: are we talking continuous batching or fixed-window batching? our product wants consistent latency for search suggestions.
[03:00] Kenji Ito: continuous batching performs better for throughput but can have more variance in tail. fixed-window gives more predictable latency at the cost of slightly worse throughput. we have an adaptive policy where small short-lived requests bypass batching for strict-interactive routes.
[03:16] Maya Singh: can we route interactive routes to hosted low-latency pool and bulk to dedicated?
[03:22] Ava Martinez: yes, hybrid routing is typical — route by route or by tag. Redwood Console supports routing policies: latency-first, cost-first, region-first. you can pin test routes to hosted for low-latency while moving background jobs to dedicated.
[03:35] Carlos Ruiz: and billing? if we mix hosted + dedicated, how does unit cost attribution work inside our invoices?
[03:41] Ava Martinez: we show per-route token-level breakdowns and cost attribution in the console. Dedicated shows committed cost and unit cost after your reserved amortization; hosted is pay-per-use. the simulator can model blended cost given percent traffic split.
[03:56] Kenji Ito: switching back to KV specifics — prefix caching: we store compressed KV vectors keyed by conversation prefix hash. prefetch warms these keys based on session activity prediction. common mis-transcripts: people think we store messages, we do not.
[04:10] Zoe Park: ok that's better — but what about encryption in transit and at rest?
[04:15] Rina Shah: we encrypt KV at rest with customer-controlled KMS keys for Private deployments, and with Redwood-managed KMS for hosted. in both cases TLS for in-flight. we also provide audit logs for cache gets/puts.
[04:29] Omar Patel: any SOC / ISO certs?
[04:32] Ava Martinez: yes SOC2 type 2 in our security pack, we also support SAML SSO and RBAC for console access. i'll share the pack after this call.
[04:44] Maya Singh: back to cost sim — can you show an extreme tail scenario? 95th percentile session length is 4x the median.
[04:52] Kenji Ito: pulling up a heavy-tail run. you can see cost per 1M tokens jumps if you keep TTL too long — because you keep many cold sessions hot consuming RAM. the sim suggests an LRU eviction policy combined with a TTL tiering (e.g., active 0–60s, warm 1–10m, cold >10m) gives best win for your profile.
[05:13] Carlos Ruiz: how do we instrument that in our app? do we need to change client SDK?
[05:19] Kenji Ito: minimal changes — use session headers and a session-id. Redwood SDKs support sessionization out of the box; the console shows per-session hit rates and you can export logs for analytics.
[05:30] Leah Bennett: what about batching heuristics per model size? we run a 13B and a 70B depending on use case.
[05:37] Kenji Ito: larger models benefit more from prefix caching (higher token compute cost), and batch sizes differ: 13B sweet spot around 4–8 concurrent requests per batch, 70B around 2–4 depending on sequence length. the simulator includes per-model kernel-efficiency factors.
[05:54] Maya Singh: do you support quantized variants on dedicated? we'd like to reduce memory for 70B.
[06:00] Rina Shah: yes, Dedicated supports Q4/Q5 quantized builds; Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profile per workload in the playbook. note quantization can slightly change generation distribution — should validate on eval sets.
[06:13] Omar Patel: any effect on cold-start time for quantized models?
[06:16] Kenji Ito: cold start can be marginally faster due to smaller footprint, but kernel warmup still matters. we show ramp charts in the console.
[06:25] Ava Martinez: quick demo of the Playbook export — you can export batching + KV recommendations and push them as config to Dedicated pools. watch me apply a canary with 10% traffic.
[06:37] Kenji Ito: note the automatic fallback: if a dedicated pool gets overloaded, requests automatically reroute to hosted compatible variants to keep the app online, that's the graceful degradation pattern.
[06:49] Zoe Park: will that affect consistency of responses? like prompt version differences?
[06:53] Kenji Ito: we do model-variant pinning and version mapping so fallback uses a compatible model family; there can be small quality deltas. the playbook flags any eval regressions when fallback occurs.
[07:07] Leah Bennett: what's the recommended first pilot?
[07:10] Ava Martinez: a two-phase pilot: 1) sandbox run with your sample traffic (7–14 days) to collect hit rates, latency, memory; 2) small dedicated pilot for heavy routes with 25–50% traffic split. we'll use the cost-sim to show expected savings before you sign up for reserved capacity.
[07:25] Maya Singh: sounds reasonable. can you run the sim for our session histogram if we upload it?
[07:29] Kenji Ito: yes, please upload via the secure link we'll send; we can run 3 scenarios and share a spreadsheet with delta breakdown per-token and amortized infra.
[07:40] Carlos Ruiz: another item — our legal will want to see data retention and deletion flow for cache keys.
[07:46] Rina Shah: we'll include that in the security pack; deletion flows exist for both hosted and private, and for private you can choose retention policies in the Console.
[07:59] Ava Martinez: ok last minute on billing: we can model blended billing with the simulator; i'll include a sample amortization for reserved GPUs in the spreadsheet.
[08:10] Maya Singh: great. any risk areas you commonly see after pilots?
[08:15] Kenji Ito: common risks: over-long TTLs causing memory pressure, misconfigured batch windows causing UX regressions, and not segmenting routes by latency needs. all fixable with the Playbook and guard rails.
[08:28] Omar Patel: what's the observability story — do we get per-token traces?
[08:31] Tomás Vega: Console has per-route token breakdown, per-request traces with sampling, and a flamegraph for kernel utilization. we can hook your tracing backend so it appears in your APM.
[08:44] Zoe Park: can we reproduce the sim locally?
[08:46] Kenji Ito: yes we provide a lightweight CLI sim that matches the Console logic; it's not exact for infra econ but helps reason about batch windows and TTLs.
[08:56] Ava Martinez: ok, let's recap. Next steps: Kenji will run the cost-sim with Ironwood's histogram, Ava will send security pack and pricing, Maya/Carlos will share traffic data and staging credentials, and we schedule the sandbox run.
[09:12] Maya Singh: thanks everyone, appreciated the clear tradeoffs. looking forward to the spreadsheet.
[09:17] Ava Martinez: thanks all — we'll follow up with links and the calendar invite. bye.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts present — e.g., kernel "warm up" transcribed as "kernel warmup" and "KV" sometimes mistranscribed as "K-V".
